You use the passive voice (la torta è stata preparata da Graziella, i fiori vengono consegnati alle dieci) and the passive "si" (si balla la tarantella) to describe preparations and ceremonies.
The church was decorated with yellow flowers.
The cake was made by Graziella.
The flowers are being delivered at ten.

To form the passive with ESSERE + participle: La torta è preparata.
To put the passive into all tenses: è stata preparata, era preparata, sarà preparata.
To introduce the agent with DA: preparata da Graziella.
To use VENIRE + participle for actions in progress: I fiori vengono consegnati.
To use the passive "si": Si vendono fiori. In Italia si mangia bene.
To describe the preparation and course of a ceremony.
Sorrento, 20th September, eight in the morning. Gennaro, the best man, is checking the list. Matei, already dressed in Ion's suit, can't keep still.
Right, let's check the list. Has the church been decorated?
Yes, last night. It was decorated with yellow flowers, as Giulia wanted.
Good. And the rings? Have they been collected from the jeweller's?
Yes, they're in my pocket. No, wait… in yours! I gave them to you yesterday!
(checks) Ah yes, here they are. Relax, brother-in-law. The cake?
The cake was made by Graziella. It arrived from Florence yesterday on the train, with Pietro holding it in his arms for three hours.
And the flowers for the reception?
They're being delivered at ten, to the hotel terrace.
And the sarmale? My grandmother has asked three times whether they've been made.
They were made by my mother and yours, together, in the hotel kitchen. The chef ran away.
(laughs) Last question: has anyone seen the bride?
No! It's bad luck. Nobody will see her before the ceremony. Not even me.
Then let's go. The ceremony will be held at eleven, and knowing my sister…
She'll be on time. She promised me.
Link the words: è-STA-ta, so-no-STA-te. Stress on "STA".
Stress on the first syllable: VEN-go-no. Not ven-GO-no!
GIO + IE: jo-yel-LYE-re, with a double LL.
The passive is formed as in Romanian: ESSERE + participle. The participle agrees with the subject.
La torta è preparata da Graziella.
La chiesa è stata decorata da Giulia.
Il matrimonio sarà celebrato dal prete.
Le sarmale erano preparate da Doina.
The agent (who does the action) is introduced with DA, which merges with the article: dal prete, dalla nonna, dai cugini.
In the passato prossimo there are TWO participles: è STATA PREPARATA. Both agree with the subject: le sarmale sono state preparate.
Instead of ESSERE you can use VENIRE (in simple tenses only). It stresses the action, not the state:
The flowers are being delivered at ten. (the act of delivering)
The door is closed every evening. (someone closes it)
Lunch was served on the terrace.
"La porta è chiusa" can mean "the door is closed" (state). "La porta viene chiusa" = someone closes it (action).
VENIRE isn't used in compound tenses: NOT "è venuta preparata".
With "si" + a 3rd-person verb you get a passive without an agent, very common in notices and descriptions. The verb agrees with the noun:
Alla festa si balla la tarantella.
At the party people dance the tarantella.
Just like Romanian: "se vinde / se vând". Easy!
The passive is used when the doer is unknown, obvious or less important than the result — for example in newspapers, invitations, instructions:
Guests are kindly asked to arrive by eleven.
The cake is made by Graziella.
The sarmale were cooked by Doina.
The wedding will take place at eleven.
The painting was restored by Matei.
In Italy people eat a lot of pasta.
La torta è stata preparata dalla nonna.
La torta ha stata preparata dalla nonna.
La torta è venuta preparata dalla nonna.
Dynamic passive: "The door is closed (by someone) every evening."
La porta viene chiusa ogni sera.
La porta ha chiuso ogni sera.
La porta si chiudono ogni sera.
Con che cosa è stata decorata la chiesa?
Da chi è stata preparata la torta?
Chi ha portato la torta in treno?

A che ora sarà celebrata la cerimonia?

On the 20th of September in Sorrento, the sky had been washed clean by the night's rain. The sea sparkled below the church of Sant'Antonino, the same one where Assunta had married seventy years earlier. By half past ten the church was already full.

On the right were the Neapolitans: a hundred and fifty uncles, cousins, neighbours and childhood friends. On the left were the Romanians: thirty people who had flown in from Sibiu, Cluj and Brașov, including Radu, introduced by Ilinca to everyone as "my boyfriend, the one with the glasses".

In the middle, in the second row, were the Florentines: Graziella in an enormous hat, Marco and Sara, Signor Franco, who had been persuaded to take the train for the first time in twenty years, and Professor Bellini, in a perfect grey suit. Pietro, with his blue watch, had been appointed "keeper of the rings". But the rings were taken back from him after ten minutes, to be on the safe side.
At five to eleven the church door was opened. A murmur ran along the pews. Giulia had arrived. On time. In fact, five minutes early. Gennaro looked at his watch and crossed himself.

She came in on her father's arm, in her great-grandmother's dress, with the mended lace veil and Doina's button. She was accompanied by the music of the organ and the eyes of three hundred people. Matei, waiting for her at the altar in Ion's suit, thought that no Renaissance painting had ever been so beautiful.

The Mass was celebrated in Italian, but the priest, who had been helped by Ilinca, also read a prayer in Romanian, with such a strong Neapolitan accent that the Romanians only understood "Doamne". When the couple said "I do", Assunta and Matei's grandmother, sitting side by side in the front row, took each other's hands.

During the signing of the register, Matei took Ernesto Bellini's tiny brush out of his pocket and placed it next to the pen. The professor saw it from the second row and had to look at the ceiling for a long time.

The reception was held on a terrace overlooking the sea. Lunch was served from two in the afternoon until eight in the evening. Neapolitan antipasti and Romanian ciorbă were eaten, spaghetti with clams and sarmale, pastiera and cozonac. Campanian wine was drunk, and Ion's pălincă, which was finished in an hour, mostly by Gennaro.

Then there was dancing. First the tarantella: the Romanians were dragged onto the dance floor by the Neapolitans, laughing and getting every step wrong. Then the hora: the Neapolitans were taken by the hand by the Romanians and spun in a big circle, faster and faster. Graziella danced with Professor Bellini. Nobody had ever seen Bellini dance. Nobody would ever forget it.

At the end of the evening Graziella's cake was cut: three tiers, yellow sugar flowers and, on top, two little marzipan figures holding hands on a beach. Like in the little painting of the bay, Signor Franco's.

Then Giulia threw the bouquet. It was caught in mid-air by a young woman with a doctor's white coat under her party dress, because she had come straight from the Sibiu hospital two days earlier: Ilinca. Radu went as red as pălincă. And Ion, from his table, raised his empty glass and said, in perfect Italian: "The next one… in Sibiu!"
